passage: Zainab, nineteen months old, heard the doorbell and pressed her face into her mother's leg. Pooja bent down, lifted her onto her lap and stayed relaxed and chatty as the neighbour came in. Zainab stared at the visitor with wide eyes, clutching Pooja's dupatta. No one pushed her for a hug. Ten minutes later, seeing her mother laughing easily, Zainab peeked out, gave a tiny wave and held out her toy rabbit. "Thank you, Zainab," the neighbour said quietly, without reaching for her, and Pooja smiled. Later Akash arrived and stretched out his arms. "Come, give uncle a kiss! Come, I will lift you up!" Zainab shook her head and turned away. Akash laughed. "Look at her acting shy!" and tried again. Zainab's lip trembled. Pooja said politely, "She doesn't feel like it today. Zainab, would you like to wave, or say namaste?" Zainab pressed her palms together and gave him a small namaste.

qa.q: What toy did Zainab hold out to the neighbour?
qa.a: She held out her toy rabbit.

qa.q: How did Zainab's behaviour with the neighbour differ from her behaviour when Akash asked for a kiss, and what did Pooja do each time?
qa.a: With the neighbour she hid and stared, then peeked, waved and offered her rabbit at her own pace once Pooja looked relaxed; with Akash, who pushed and laughed, she shook her head and her lip trembled, so Pooja backed her and offered a wave or namaste.

qa.q: What was Zainab probably feeling when Akash laughed at her refusal?
qa.a: She was uneasy and upset, since her lip trembled and she turned away, as if her no did not count.

qa.q: What could Pooja do the next time a relative pushes for a kiss?
qa.a: She could keep politely backing Zainab and offering a wave or namaste instead, without forcing any contact.

grounding: One toddler shows fear of a visitor, curiosity once her mother is at ease, and a relative who ignores her refusal until her mother backs her.

passage: Reena's flat share with Varun had begun to feel like a battlefield. Dishes sat for days, his music thumped after midnight, and her charger was gone again. For weeks she said nothing, then left him a sticky note that said, "Some people were raised in barns." It ended in a shouting match. Ashamed, she waited a week and asked him at a calm time: "Three things bother me: dishes by the next morning, headphones after eleven, and asking before you borrow. Can we write a rota?" Varun, red-faced, agreed. She also caught herself wrinkling her nose at the smell of his fish curry and at his morning prayer chanting. She asked herself whether this was a real problem or only a difference. Only the dishes and the noise were real, so she let the rest go. Then some money vanished from her drawer. She did not accuse anyone. She wrote down when she had last seen it, asked Varun casually if he had noticed anything, and told Tejas, the landlord, who changed the lock and kept a note of the dates.

qa.q: What three things did Reena ask Varun about at the calm time?
qa.a: She asked about dishes by the next morning, headphones after eleven, and asking before he borrows.

qa.q: How did Reena's first attempt to raise the problem differ from her second?
qa.a: First she said nothing for weeks and then left a sticky note that ended in a shouting match; the second time she spoke at a calm time, named three specific things and proposed a rota.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling about the smell of the fish curry and the prayer chanting, and what did she decide?
qa.a: She felt irritated, but she asked herself whether it was a real problem or only a difference, and she let it go.

qa.q: What could Reena do if something goes missing again?
qa.a: She could keep writing down the facts, talk to Varun calmly and involve Tejas, rather than accuse anyone without evidence.

grounding: One flat share brings anger over dishes and noise, a calm talk, irritation at differences and missing money handled without accusation.

passage: Sumit had sent the team's report without Nazia's section, and she lost marks because of it. For two days he argued, listing reasons why it was not really his fault, because admitting it felt like admitting he was nothing. Then Nazia stopped answering his messages. The silence sat like a weight on his chest. His mentor Rukmini heard him out and said, "I did much worse at your age. So what is your move?" He felt steadied, and he did not hear it as a licence to slack off; he set alarms for every future deadline. That night he stood at the mirror and said aloud, "I got this wrong, and I still deserve respect, from me too." It made the next step easier. He wrote to Nazia: "I am sorry. I sent it without your section and it cost you marks. No excuses. I will speak to the professor about a resubmission if you want. I won't push you to reply." Nazia did not answer that week. He left it, and kept his promise about the deadlines.

qa.q: Whose section did Sumit leave out of the report?
qa.a: He left out Nazia's section.

qa.q: How did Sumit's first reaction to his mistake differ from what he did after talking with Rukmini?
qa.a: At first he argued with reasons why it was not his fault; after Rukmini's question and his words at the mirror, he wrote a clear apology with no excuses and offered to speak to the professor.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when Nazia stopped answering his messages?
qa.a: He felt guilty, with the silence sitting like a weight on his chest.

qa.q: What could Sumit do while waiting for Nazia to reply?
qa.a: He could give her space without pressing for forgiveness and keep his promise about deadlines.

grounding: After a mistake that harmed a teammate, a young man moves from defensive pride to a mentor's steadying words, self-respect and an apology that gives the other person space.

passage: Pankaj followed Coach Bhupen's every word and lived for his nod. When he was benched for the semi-final, he burned. He told a teammate the coach obviously preferred others and nearly quit that night. In the morning he asked, "What should I fix to get back in?" Bhupen said, "Your footwork against the short ball, and your temper." Pankaj trained on it. Loving the coach's words, he had also started to ask why behind each one. Meanwhile a senior, Rohit, was using Pankaj's scorebook analysis for a school competition while promising to introduce him to a scout. Weeks passed and nothing came. Pankaj noticed the imbalance. "What exactly will you do with my sheets, and when?" he asked. Rohit dodged, so Pankaj went to the maths teacher, who knew a real analyst, and asked for advice there too. In the nets, Baljeet, a Class 6 boy, copied Pankaj's hairstyle and the way he tapped his bat. Pankaj grinned, then said, "I dropped a catch last week. Don't copy that part. Find your own style."

qa.q: What did Pankaj ask Coach Bhupen after being benched?
qa.a: He asked what he should fix to get back in.

qa.q: How did Pankaj's response to being benched differ from his handling of Rohit's promises?
qa.a: After being benched he nearly quit, then asked the coach what to fix and trained on it; with Rohit he noticed the imbalance, asked clear questions and sought another mentor.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when he was benched for the semi-final?
qa.a: He felt resentful and hurt, believing the coach preferred others.

qa.q: What could Pankaj keep doing for Baljeet?
qa.a: He could keep admitting his own flaws and encouraging Baljeet to find his own style, instead of enjoying the copying.

grounding: A teen athlete's relationships with a coach and a senior show devotion, resentment at being benched, exploitation by a mentor and being idolised by a younger boy.

passage: At the shop, Leela pointed at a shiny toy car and wailed when her mother, Ishita, said no. "We have money for the fruit today," Ishita said calmly, and she did not buy it to stop the crying. Leela sniffled, then let herself be led out. At home she tipped her piggy bank onto the bed and counted her coins into little piles, feeling proud that she was waiting for a paint set. Then her older sister Afreen received a bigger weekly coin because she was ten, and Leela cried, "It's not fair!" Ishita explained, "Each of you gets more as you grow. When you are ten you will get the same, and each of you can spend or save your own." Leela nodded, still sniffling. At school her friend Tanish showed a huge robot toy. Leela felt a sting and said, "My toy is better!" On the way home she told her mother, "We are poor." Ishita took her hand. "We each have different things, and we have enough."

qa.q: What did Leela count at home?
qa.a: She counted the coins from her piggy bank.

qa.q: How did Ishita handle Leela's begging at the shop compared with Leela's upset about Afreen's bigger weekly coin?
qa.a: At the shop she calmly said there was money for fruit and did not buy the toy to stop the crying; about Afreen's coin she explained that each child gets more as they grow and can spend or save their own.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she said "My toy is better!"?
qa.a: She felt a sting of envy, wanting a robot toy like Tanish's.

qa.q: What could Ishita do to help Leela keep saving?
qa.a: She could praise Leela's patience, count coins with her, and remind her that the paint set gets closer with each coin. 🙂

grounding: A five-year-old meets money through a refused toy, pride in saving, a sister's larger allowance and envy of a friend's toy.

passage: Jahnavi no longer believed in some of the rituals, yet she sat beside her Ajji at evening prayer every day, letting the old woman's hand rest on hers. She never smirked; she kept her doubts inside. The temple was also home: her friends, her tabla class, the smell of jasmine. One Sunday she asked the elder, Tejas, why they did a particular ritual. His face hardened. "That is disrespect," he said, and over the next weeks some families stopped greeting her. It hurt deeply. She thought of leaving altogether, but Salma, who ran the youth group's community kitchen, said, "Ask me anything. Not every elder thinks like that." Jahnavi began serving meals with Salma on Sundays and found that passing plates, then sitting quietly for five minutes afterwards, steadied her and made her kinder to the shy new girl at the counter. She kept asking her questions, kept sitting beside her grandmother, and kept her friends.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do with Salma on Sundays?
qa.a: She served meals at the community kitchen.

qa.q: How did Tejas's reaction to Jahnavi's question differ from Salma's, and how did Jahnavi respond?
qa.a: Tejas called the question disrespect and some families stopped greeting her, which hurt, while Salma invited her to ask anything, and Jahnavi began serving meals with Salma.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when families stopped greeting her?
qa.a: She felt hurt and rejected, deeply enough that she thought of leaving altogether.

qa.q: How can Jahnavi honour her grandmother while staying honest about her doubts?
qa.a: She can keep sitting beside her grandmother at prayer without mocking, keep her questions respectful, and take them to people who welcome them.

grounding: A teenager's doubts about family faith sit beside love for a grandmother, belonging at the temple, steadying service and an elder's rejection.
